reason: Reconcile the HCC clinical source check and cross-disease comparisons; correct allocation wording, endpoint direction, study populations and limits. Preserve existing treatment decision hierarchy and review status.

edits.old: Multiphase liver CT or MRI; transplant-radiology review of adequacy and at-risk liver context.
edits.new: Measure lesions on pretreatment multiphase liver CT or MRI. An eligible lesion can meet OPTN Class 5 by LI-RADS 5 CT, MRI or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, or by biopsy. Stage vascular invasion and extrahepatic spread with CT or MRI.

edits.old: Schedule multiphase CT/MRI and AFP; NLRB guidance advises imaging ≥4 weeks after the last downstaging treatment.
edits.new: Obtain multiphase liver CT or MRI and AFP after LRT to assess viable T2 burden. For a nonstandard request after starting beyond UNOS-DS, NLRB guidance advises imaging at least four weeks after the last treatment.

edits.old: HCC guidance
edits.new: HCC guidance · individual requests after initial burden beyond standard downstaging criteria

edits.old: Record the treatment goal, anatomical and liver-function considerations, and response-imaging date. Ask transplant radiology to resolve uncertain residual tumor before changing treatment.
edits.new: Record the treatment goal, anatomical and liver-function considerations, and response-imaging date. Ask transplant radiology to resolve uncertain residual tumor before changing treatment. The four-week guidance applies to an individual NLRB request for a patient initially beyond standard downstaging entry criteria.

edits.old: Five-year competing-risk cumulative recurrence: 9.5%, 20.5%, 40.5% for low/intermediate/high NYCA categories. Discrimination C statistic 0.66. These are composite-score categories, not isolated AFP ranges. Recipient selection, exclusion of early deaths, no waitlist dropout or transplant-benefit comparison. Maximum-to-final AFP can miss a rebound below the original peak. Extreme-AFP response subgroup was tiny. Full PDF saved privately; TMC: https://libkey.io/libraries/480/10.1001/jamasurg.2021.0954

edits.old: Retrospective multisite cohort. Solitary HCC ≤8 cm; RS 57 versus resection 66. Target progression 5% versus 8%; adjusted overall-progression HR 1.16 (95% CI 0.51–2.63). Median OS not reached in either group. Propensity distributions were too dissimilar to match. Different surgical candidacy and liver function prevent a claim of equivalence to resection. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: RS vs resection; solitary HCC ≤8 cm. Unadjusted time to any progression 21.9 vs 29.4 mo (P=.03). Adjusted progression HR 1.16 (0.51–2.63). Median OS unreached in both groups. Retrospective; inadequate overlap prevented propensity matching. Not evidence of equivalence.

edits.old: National observational cohort. 31,609 US HCC transplant candidates, 2003–2018; 24,145 received LRT. IPTW-adjusted dropout sHR versus TACE: radioembolization 0.85 (95% CI 0.81–0.89); thermal ablation 0.95 (0.91–0.99). Observational first-treatment comparison, with later treatments allowed. Center, era and patient selection remain confounders. Registry cohorts overlap with later studies. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: Initial LRT in 31,609 OPTN HCC candidates. Dropout sHR for Y90 and ablation vs TACE: IPTW 0.85 and 0.95, conventional adjustment 1.03 (0.91–1.17) and 0.97 (0.90–1.05), respectively. Observational. Modality associations varied with the adjustment method. Center and era may confound.

edits.old: Prospective multicenter cohort. MERITS-LT: 326 within UNOS-DS and 190 all-comers beyond UNOS-DS; 2015–2023. In the all-comers subgroup, 2-year successful downstaging was 74% with initial Y90 versus 65% with TACE (p<0.001). Treatment was not randomized; subgroup finding does not expand allocation criteria. Overlaps earlier MERITS-LT enrollment. Earlier within-UNOS-DS study found no significant modality difference. Available main text checked for the stated results.
edits.new: Initial Y90 vs TACE within or beyond UNOS downstaging entry criteria. 2-y downstaging, Y90 vs TACE: 73.8% vs 64.6% beyond UNOS-DS, 78.1% vs 86.5% within. First therapy was not predictive after center stratification (P=.07). Treatment was nonrandomized, and this cohort overlaps MERITS-LT. Allocation criteria still apply.

edits.old: Randomized study. 70 early HCC patients: cisplatin HAIC before RFA versus RFA alone, 35 per arm. 3-year RFS 54.3% versus 34.3%; HR 0.597 (95% CI 0.320–1.091), p=0.094. Primary RFS endpoint was not significant. A secondary distant-intrahepatic recurrence signal does not establish routine HAIC addition or HAIC as a replacement for ablation. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: Cisplatin HAIC before RFA vs RFA; 70 patients. Three-year RFS 54.3% vs 34.3%; HR 0.597 (0.320–1.091), p=0.094. Primary RFS comparison was inconclusive. The distant intrahepatic recurrence analysis was post hoc.

edits.old: Randomized phase III. 74 patients with bilobar unresectable CRLM: Y90 plus regional FUDR versus regional FUDR alone. Tumor-volume response 50% versus 24% (p=0.03); liver progression was delayed. Tests adding Y90 to HAI, not Y90 versus HAI alone. Older chemotherapy era; no established overall-survival benefit. Not evidence against ablation of small lesions. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: Y90+regional FUDR vs FUDR; randomized CRLM trial. Tumor-volume response 50% vs 24%; delayed liver progression. Closed at 74 of 95 planned. Endpoints shifted from survival to response and progression. No proven OS gain.

edits.old: Prematurely stopped randomized trial (HARVEST). 92 randomized after CRLM surgery; modified ITT 77, HAI-FUDR plus systemic 38 versus systemic 39. 3-year RFS 31.4% versus 34.4%, p=0.28. Stopped for FUDR supply shortage; primary endpoint negative. Exploratory early-RFS/subgroup signals do not establish routine postoperative HAI. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: HARVEST: postop FUDR HAI+systemic vs systemic. Three-year RFS 31.4% vs 34.4% (p=0.28). Allocation moved after resection following the first 11 patients. FUDR shortage closed enrollment.

edits.old: Retrospective comparison. 319 multifocal iCCA patients: unresectable HAIP-FUDR 141 versus resection 178 across different centers/eras. Median OS 20.3 versus 18.9 months; adjusted HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.55–1.03), p=0.07. HAIP patients had substantially more bilobar/multifocal disease. Not an equivalence trial or reason to deny resection to an otherwise suitable patient; does not distinguish all satellites from metastases. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: Pump HAI vs resection; multifocal iCCA. OS 20.3 vs 18.9 mo; adjusted HR 0.75 (0.55–1.03). All were multifocal. HAIP vs resection: bilobar 88.0% vs 34.3%, ≥4 lesions 66.7% vs 24.2%.

edits.old: Retrospective NCDB comparison. Main-text analysis: SBRT 27, chemoradiation 54, TARE 60; nonmetastatic node-negative unresected iCCA. Adjusted OS HR 0.42 (95% CI 0.21–0.84) for SBRT versus TARE. TARE tumors were larger/more often multifocal or vascular-invasive. Strong selection bias and abstract/main-text cohort-count discrepancy; not causal superiority or equivalent treatment eligibility. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: SBRT vs TARE in unresected iCCA; NCDB cohort. SBRT vs TARE, OS: multivariable HR 0.42 (0.21–0.84). IPTW HR 0.58 (0.37–0.91), P=.019, above the prespecified Bonferroni threshold of .017. Registry cohort. Tumor burden and vascular invasion differed.

edits.old: Retrospective two-center cohort. 248 NELM patients: TARE 51 versus TACE 197. Initial DCR 83% versus 96% (p<0.01); no significant OS or PFS difference. TARE was usually outpatient. Nonrandomized baseline and treatment-selection differences. Does not prove equivalence; treatment burden and delayed toxicity also matter. Full-text design and key outcomes checked, 4 November 2026.
edits.new: TARE vs TACE; 248 patients with NELM. TARE vs TACE: initial disease control 83% vs 96% (P<.01), with no significant OS or PFS difference. Retrospective, nonrandomized groups. The disease-control association does not demonstrate a survival benefit.

edits.old: Assess viable tumor separately from the treated cavity and retain pretreatment stage. For downstaging, guidance advises imaging ≥4 weeks after the last treatment.
edits.new: Assess viable tumor separately from the treated cavity and retain pretreatment stage. For a nonstandard request after starting beyond UNOS-DS, NLRB guidance advises imaging at least four weeks after the last treatment.

edits.old: Vp1 five-year OS 69.5%, DFS 56.2%; Vp4 OS 50.0%, DFS 34.3%. Exact Vp2/Vp3 five-year values were not tabulated. Vp4 recurrence was 9/14 (64.3%) by Table 2 count, not a five-year risk. Responders: 83 patients, five-year OS 66.6%, DFS 64.7%, recurrence 28/83; nonresponders: 54, OS 35.1%, DFS 19.7%, recurrence 42/54. Viable PVTT remained in 65/83 responder explants.
edits.new: Vp1 five-year OS 69.5%, DFS 56.2%; Vp4 OS 50.0%, DFS 34.3%. Exact Vp2/Vp3 five-year values were not tabulated. Vp4 recurrence was 9/14 (64.3%) by Table 2 count, not a five-year risk. Responders: 83 patients, five-year OS 66.6%, DFS 64.7%, recurrence 28/83; nonresponders: 54, OS 35.1%, DFS 19.7%, recurrence 42/54. Viable PVTT remained in 65/83 responders at the time of LDLT (Table 1 does not specify the assessment method).

edits.old: Biopsy-proven rejection 9/48 (18.8%) versus 28/144 (19.4%), P=.916. Two exposed cases were steroid resistant; one rejection-related graft failure required retransplant. Overall graft failure 2/48 versus 3/144, retransplant 2 versus zero, recurrence 5/48 versus 15/144, death 7/48 versus 21/144. Median follow-up 2.6 versus 3.2 years. Table 1 washout median 60 days, IQR 22–196.
edits.new: Rejection occurred in 9/48 ICI recipients (18.8%, all biopsy-proven) and 28/144 controls (19.4%, biopsy or clinical response to steroids), P=.916. Two exposed cases were steroid resistant; one rejection-related graft failure required retransplant. Overall graft failure 2/48 versus 3/144, retransplant 2 versus zero, recurrence 5/48 versus 15/144, death 7/48 versus 21/144. Median follow-up 2.6 versus 3.2 years. Table 1 washout median 60 days, IQR 22–196.

edits.old: Ablation and selected Y90 radiation segmentectomy can both have curative intent. Choose by tumor size, location, liver reserve, achievable ablation margin or segmental dosimetry. Ablation has more randomized comparative evidence. Y90 versus ablation studies are mainly observational. Y90 is associated with less waitlist dropout than TACE in registry analyses, but no dedicated randomized comparison establishes a transplant or survival advantage.
edits.new: Ablation and selected Y90 radiation segmentectomy can both have curative intent. Choose by tumor size, location, liver reserve, achievable ablation margin or segmental dosimetry. Ablation has more randomized comparative evidence. Y90 versus ablation studies are mainly observational. Some registry analyses associate Y90 with less dropout than TACE. Estimates vary by adjustment method, and downstaging results differ by baseline tumor burden. No randomized trial establishes a transplant or survival advantage.

      "evidence": "EMERALD-1, LEAP-012 and EMERALD-3 reported progression-free survival benefit for their respective combinations. In EMERALD-3, STRIDE + lenvatinib + TACE yielded PFS 13.0 versus 9.8 months; overall-survival superiority was not established at the reported analysis.",
      "limits": "PFS benefit is not proof of OS benefit or a transplant bridge. LEAP-012 grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicity was 71% vs 32%; EMERALD-3 grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity was 63% vs 19%. EMERALD-1 durvalumab without bevacizumab did not improve PFS.",
      "transplant": "For a listed patient with treatable liver-limited disease, use LRT for routine bridging. Adding systemic treatment has no demonstrated benefit for dropout or transplant receipt. In embolization-eligible unresectable HCC, reported follow-up showed median overall survival of 40.4 vs 40.8 months in LEAP-012 (HR 0.98) and 29.9 vs 33.3 months in EMERALD-1 (HR 1.10). Neither trial measured waitlist dropout or transplant receipt.

ys/assets/portal-navigation.css?v=20261109-pathology1">

Roadmaps / Treatment matrices · systemic therapy by tumor type

Systemic therapy matrix

Choose a tumor and a treatment setting. Each card shows when to consider a regimen and its trial results, with every PMID linked to the full citation; open Limits, Transplant or Sources for the rest.

Multidisciplinary review aid, not prescribing orders. Cross-trial survival medians do not rank treatments.

Clinical review draft · Evidence reviewed through 25 October 2026.

Choose by tumor type, stage, prior treatment, biomarkers, organ function and patient goals. Trial results retain their own populations and comparators; cross-trial survival medians do not rank treatments. This matrix supports multidisciplinary discussion and does not provide prescribing orders.

Settings

Colour marks the treatment setting — its place in the treatment sequence. It is not an evidence grade or a ranking.

Treatment options by setting

Initial advanced-disease treatment

Atezolizumab + bevacizumab

HCC
Preferred first-line option

When to consider. Unresectable HCC requiring systemic treatment; strongest evidence in Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1. Assess and treat high-risk varices before bevacizumab.

Clinical evidence.
  • IMbrave150: updated median overall survival 19.2 versus 13.4 months with sorafenib; HR 0.66.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Bleeding, portal hypertension, blood pressure, proteinuria and immune toxicity affect selection. Do not compare its survival median directly with a different trial.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. If transplant remains possible, review the plan before the first dose. Record both last-dose dates and agree how to handle an early graft offer. Pretransplant series describe selected downstaging and a risk of rejection.

Trials and supporting sources (2)
  • IMbrave150 · Finn · New England Journal of Medicine · 2020PMID 32402160 · DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1915745 · TMC Library
  • IMbrave150 update · Cheng · Journal of Hepatology · 2022PMID 34902530 · DOI 10.1016/j.jhep.2021.11.030 · TMC Library

Durvalumab + tremelimumab (STRIDE)

HCC
Preferred first-line option

When to consider. Unresectable HCC, preserved liver function and fitness for dual checkpoint therapy. An option when bevacizumab is unsuitable and immunotherapy is appropriate.

Clinical evidence.
  • HIMALAYA: median overall survival 16.43 versus 13.77 months with sorafenib; HR 0.78. Progression-free survival was not significantly improved.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Main portal-vein invasion was excluded from the pivotal trial. Immune toxicity remains important; avoiding bevacizumab does not remove treatment risk.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. Requires a transplant-specific plan if transplantation may later be considered.

Trials and supporting sources (1)
  • HIMALAYA / STRIDE · Abou-Alfa · NEJM Evidence · 2022PMID 38319892 · DOI 10.1056/EVIDoa2100070 · TMC Library

Nivolumab + ipilimumab

HCC
Preferred first-line option

When to consider. Unresectable HCC; select patients able to tolerate dual checkpoint therapy and close early monitoring.

Clinical evidence.
  • CheckMate 9DW: median overall survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months with lenvatinib or sorafenib; HR 0.79.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Survival curves crossed: mortality was higher during the first six months (HR 1.65). Grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 41% versus 42%; treatment-related deaths were 12 versus 3.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. Review future transplant intent and immune adverse effects before choosing this regimen.

Trials and supporting sources (1)
  • CheckMate 9DW · Yau · The Lancet · 2025PMID 40349714 · DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(25)00403-9 · TMC Library

Single-agent checkpoint therapy

HCC
Selected alternative

When to consider. Tislelizumab or durvalumab when a single-agent approach is appropriate. NCCN HCC v2.2026 also lists pembrolizumab first line, category 2B.

Clinical evidence.
  • RATIONALE-301 established overall-survival noninferiority of tislelizumab to sorafenib.
  • HIMALAYA established noninferiority of durvalumab.
  • KEYNOTE-394 supported later-line pembrolizumab in an Asian population;
  • KEYNOTE-240 did not meet its prespecified statistical thresholds.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Guideline options and US indications differ: durvalumab monotherapy is not the labelled HCC regimen; the HCC label specifies combination treatment. KEYNOTE-240/394 are later-line studies, not first-line superiority evidence.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. Single-agent checkpoint therapy still carries transplant rejection concerns.

Trials and supporting sources (4)
  • RATIONALE-301 · Qin · JAMA Oncology · 2023PMID 37796513 · DOI 10.1001/jamaoncol.2023.4003 · TMC Library
  • HIMALAYA / STRIDE · Abou-Alfa · NEJM Evidence · 2022PMID 38319892 · DOI 10.1056/EVIDoa2100070 · TMC Library
  • KEYNOTE-240 · Finn · J Clin Oncol · 2020PMID 31790344 · DOI 10.1200/JCO.19.01307 · TMC Library
  • KEYNOTE-394 · Qin · Journal of Clinical Oncology · 2023PMID 36455168 · DOI 10.1200/JCO.22.00620 · TMC Library

Lenvatinib or sorafenib

HCC
Alternative when immunotherapy is unsuitable

When to consider. Unresectable HCC with adequate liver reserve; consider when checkpoint therapy is contraindicated or inconsistent with the transplant plan.

Clinical evidence.
  • REFLECT: lenvatinib vs sorafenib OS 13.6 vs 12.3 months; noninferiority design.
  • SHARP: sorafenib vs placebo OS 10.7 vs 7.9 months, HR 0.69 (0.55–0.87); radiologic time to progression 5.5 vs 2.8 months, not PFS.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. REFLECT enrolled Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1 and excluded main portal-vein invasion, ≥50% liver occupation and obvious bile-duct invasion. SHARP reported grade 3 diarrhea and hand–foot reaction of 8% each with sorafenib; these are not lenvatinib toxicity rates. Little evidence supports use in decompensated cirrhosis.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. When local treatment is infeasible or has failed, review systemic treatment with the transplant team. In two small bridging trials, adding sorafenib to TACE or Y90 showed no clear transplant benefit. In the Y90 pilot, all 10 sorafenib patients needed a dose reduction. Biliary complications within 30 days occurred in 4/8 combination recipients vs 0/9 with Y90 alone.

Trials and supporting sources (4)
  • REFLECT · Kudo · The Lancet · 2018PMID 29433850 · DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30207-1 · TMC Library
  • SHARP: sorafenib · Llovet · New England Journal of Medicine · 2008PMID 18650514 · DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0708857 · TMC Library

Kulik et al. · Y90 with or without sorafenib · PMID 24681342

HeiLivCa · TACE with sorafenib or placebo · PMID 25957784

Gemcitabine + cisplatin + durvalumab or pembrolizumab

pCCA / iCCA
Preferred first-line options

When to consider. Unresectable or metastatic biliary cancer after addressing biliary obstruction, infection, renal function and performance status.

Clinical evidence.
  • TOPAZ-1: overall-survival HR 0.80 for durvalumab + chemotherapy versus chemotherapy.
  • KEYNOTE-966: median overall survival 12.7 versus 10.9 months, HR 0.83, with pembrolizumab added.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Mixed biliary-tract populations; neither trial establishes a separate pCCA-specific effect or superiority between these two checkpoint regimens. ASCO 2026.1.0 is an advanced-BTC systemic guideline, not a transplant-neoadjuvant or eligibility guideline.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. For potentially transplant-eligible pCCA or iCCA, obtain transplant-program review first. Palliative chemoimmunotherapy is not an interchangeable transplant neoadjuvant protocol.

Trials and supporting sources (3)
  • TOPAZ-1 · Oh DY · NEJM evidence · 2022PMID 38319896 · DOI 10.1056/EVIDoa2200015 · TMC Library
  • KEYNOTE-966 · Kelley RK · Lancet (London, England) · 2023PMID 37075781 · DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00727-4 · TMC Library
  • ASCO BTC living guideline 2026.1.0 · Shroff RT · Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology · 2026PMID 42874012 · DOI 10.1200/JCO-26-02462 · TMC Library

Gemcitabine + cisplatin; adapt intensity when necessary

pCCA / iCCA
When checkpoint therapy is unsuitable

When to consider. Use chemotherapy alone when immunotherapy is unsuitable. Renal impairment, neuropathy, hearing loss or frailty may require a different platinum, regimen or single agent after oncology review.

Clinical evidence.
  • ABC-02 established cisplatin–gemcitabine over gemcitabine: median overall survival 11.7 versus 8.1 months; HR 0.64.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Alternative platinum substitutions and dose reductions do not reproduce the exact ABC-02 evidence. Treat infection and improve drainage before reassessing fitness. ASCO 2026.1.0 is an advanced-BTC systemic guideline, not a transplant-neoadjuvant or eligibility guideline.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. An approved transplant regimen may use chemotherapy differently; confirm the protocol before starting treatment.

    Limits of the evidence. Long-term risks include marrow toxicity and uncommon myelodysplasia/leukemia. Primary site and prior therapy affect applicability. NETTER-1 enrolled midgut NET; its numerical results are not pancreatic-NET-specific estimates.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Record disease control and treatment toxicity before any transplant benefit review. PRRT response does not expand accepted grade or spread criteria.

    Everolimus or sunitinib

    NELM / pNET
    Progressive disease; primary site determines the option

    When to consider. Everolimus: pancreatic NET or appropriate nonfunctional GI/lung NET. Sunitinib: pancreatic NET.

    Clinical evidence.
    • RADIANT-3: PFS 11.0 versus 4.6 months in pancreatic NET.
    • RADIANT-4: PFS 11.0 versus 3.9 months in nonfunctional GI/lung NET.
    • Sunitinib trial: PFS 11.4 versus 5.5 months in pancreatic NET.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Trials used placebo comparators, not contemporary PRRT/CAPTEM sequencing. Monitor infection/pneumonitis/metabolic toxicity with everolimus and vascular/cardiac toxicity with sunitinib.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. The efficacy of nontransplant options must be considered before exposing a recipient and donor to transplantation.

    Cabozantinib

    NELM / pNET
    Previously treated, progressive well-differentiated NET

    When to consider. Pancreatic or extrapancreatic NET after appropriate prior treatment.

    Clinical evidence.
    • CABINET: median PFS 13.8 versus 4.4 months in pancreatic NET and 8.4 versus 3.9 months in extrapancreatic NET, each compared with placebo.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. The two cohorts are distinct; do not pool their effect sizes. Toxicity and dose reductions are common. PFS benefit does not establish an OS advantage.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. An additional effective nontransplant option changes the benefit discussion, not the transplant criteria.

    Trials and supporting sources (1)
    • CABINET · Chan JA · The New England journal of medicine · 2025PMID 39282913 · DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2403991 · TMC Library

    Liposomal irinotecan fluorouracil leucovorin or switch backbone — Subsequent treatment

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. nal-IRI plus 5-FU/LV after gemcitabine-based therapy when eligible. Gemcitabine-based therapy may follow a fluoropyrimidine regimen. Account for prior irinotecan and residual neuropathy. Use the combination after gemcitabine when fit; avoid treating nal-IRI as interchangeable with conventional irinotecan. Dose conventions differ: 70 mg/m² free base equals 80 mg/m² salt in the publication. Pharmacy must verify the actual product/order set.

    Clinical evidence.
    • nal-IRI plus 5-FU/LV: OS 6.1 versus 4.2 months, HR 0.67 (0.49–0.92); PFS 3.1 versus 1.5, HR 0.56. ORR 16% versus 1%. nal-IRI monotherapy did not improve OS (HR 0.99). Grade 3–4 neutropenia 27%, diarrhea 13%.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Small prior-irinotecan subgroup, different 5-FU schedules, selected organ function. No validated immediate reuse after FOLFIRINOX/NALIRIFOX. One combination treatment-related septic-shock death.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. This is a cancer-treatment roadmap update only. The withdrawn PDAC liver-transplant pathway remains closed; chemotherapy response does not reopen it.

    • ESMO_PDAC · Conroy T · Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology · 2023PMID 37678671 · DOI 10.1016/j.annonc.2023.08.009 · TMC Library

    Liposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil leucovorin — Selected later line

    iCCA / pCCA
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Discuss only with an explicit explanation of the inconsistent randomized evidence, prior irinotecan exposure, bilirubin and diarrhea risk. Not an interchangeable default with FOLFOX. Show NALIRICC alongside NIFTY. Do not call nal-IRI/5-FU an unqualified preferred second-line BTC regimen. Consider only a qualified alternative after target review, especially if oxaliplatin is unsuitable, with explicit benefit/toxicity discussion.

    Clinical evidence.
    • PFS 2.6 versus 2.3 months, HR 0.87 (0.56–1.35); OS 6.9 versus 8.2 months, HR 1.08 (0.68–1.72). ORR 14% versus 4% did not translate into PFS/OS benefit. Grade ≥3 events 71% versus 50%; treatment-related serious events 33% versus 2%.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Small phase II trial; subsequent therapy differed (more control patients received later therapy). This does not erase the negative primary PFS result. Contrasts with positive NIFTY; population and treatment differences do not resolve the inconsistency.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Systemic disease control is not proof of transplant benefit. Preserve the route-specific histology, liver-only status, unresectability and observation gates. A cHCC-CCA component changes the evidence base; use expert pathology review.

    NELM / pNET
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Consider FOLFIRI, FOLFOX, selected temozolomide-based treatment or a trial according to prior exposure, pathology and pace. Supportive care may be the best option when toxicity exceeds likely benefit.

    Clinical evidence.
    • Later-line NEC evidence is limited; no universally superior sequence. Do not import PRRT or NET targeted-drug results into receptor-negative poorly differentiated NEC.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Evidence and label requirements vary by regimen and setting; confirm the source and pharmacy plan.

    Transplant implications. A cancer treatment response does not by itself establish transplant candidacy.

    PDAC
    Subsequent treatment; broader label includes patients unfit for multiagent therapy

    When to consider. US approval August 2026: metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one prior systemic treatment or when not a candidate for multiagent systemic therapy. The indication is not restricted to a RAS mutation.

    Clinical evidence.
    • RASolute 302 randomized previously treated patients: overall-population OS 13.2 versus 6.7 months, HR 0.40. That trial does not independently establish the same effect in treatment-naive frail patients included in the broader label.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Evidence and label requirements vary by regimen and setting; confirm the source and pharmacy plan.

    Transplant implications. This is a cancer-treatment roadmap update only. The withdrawn PDAC liver-transplant pathway remains closed; chemotherapy response does not reopen it.

    FDA approves daraxonrasib for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma

    Around curative local treatment

    After curative resection or ablation

    HCC
    Surveillance; avoid routine adjuvant atezolizumab–bevacizumab

    When to consider. No residual HCC after resection or ablation; IMbrave050 enrolled patients at high recurrence risk.

    Clinical evidence.
    • IMbrave050 initially reported a recurrence-free survival advantage. The 2026 update did not sustain that result: RFS HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.72–1.12); overall survival remained immature. Updated OS HR 1.26; immature survival data do not establish benefit or harm.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. The updated evidence does not support routine adjuvant atezolizumab–bevacizumab. Trial participation remains an option.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Continue surveillance and reassess recurrent disease through the standard pathway.

    Capecitabine after resection

    pCCA / iCCA
    Usual adjuvant discussion

    When to consider. Resected biliary cancer after recovery; discuss approximately six months of adjuvant treatment and margin-specific radiation considerations.

    Clinical evidence.
    • BILCAP: primary intention-to-treat overall-survival comparison was not significant (HR 0.81; p=0.097); prespecified sensitivity and per-protocol analyses favored capecitabine.
    • ASCOT supported S-1 in a Japanese population.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Do not describe BILCAP as an unequivocally positive primary-endpoint trial. PRODIGE-12 and BCAT did not establish adjuvant GEMOX or gemcitabine benefit. S-1 applicability and access differ by region.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Adjuvant treatment after resection and neoadjuvant treatment before transplant are separate settings.

    Perioperative chemotherapy around liver resection

    CRLM
    Individualize with the liver multidisciplinary team

    When to consider. Resectable CRLM: balance recurrence risk, prior treatment, liver injury and surgical timing. Surgery-first or perioperative chemotherapy may be appropriate.

    Clinical evidence.
    • EORTC 40983 showed PFS signals in eligible/resected analyses; its intention-to-treat PFS comparison and long-term OS comparison were not significant.
    • New EPOC found worse OS when cetuximab was added to perioperative chemotherapy.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Do not use metastatic anti-EGFR response data to justify routine perioperative cetuximab for resectable CRLM. Exploratory molecular subtypes from New EPOC are not validated selectors for transplantation.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Resectability is reviewed before a transplant route. Radiographic disappearance alone does not prove eradication.

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Fit patient recovered after R0/R1 resection, with adequate performance status and organ function. Plan approximately six months, adjusted for prior neoadjuvant exposure and recovery.

    Clinical evidence.
    • PRODIGE 24 provides randomized survival evidence over gemcitabine in selected postoperative patients. It does not establish tolerability in every postoperative patient or prove neoadjuvant superiority.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Evidence and label requirements vary by regimen and setting; confirm the source and pharmacy plan.

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. GemCap when mFOLFIRINOX is unsuitable; gemcitabine or a fluoropyrimidine for patients unable to tolerate a combination. Check renal function, hand-foot toxicity and fluoropyrimidine safety.

    Clinical evidence.
    • ESPAC-4 supports GemCap over gemcitabine; these are PDAC trials. Applying them to ampullary or mixed histology is extrapolation, not direct evidence.

    Limits of the evidence. Evidence and label requirements vary by regimen and setting; confirm the source and pharmacy plan.

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Tissue-confirmed borderline resectable or locally advanced disease after MDT review; define anatomical and biological reassessment points. Clearly resectable PDAC needs a separate surgery-first versus neoadjuvant discussion.

    Clinical evidence.
    • A021501 supports a chemotherapy-first approach in its borderline-resectable setting but is not a definitive head-to-head proof against all radiation.
    • NORPACT-1 did not establish benefit of routine neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX in resectable pancreatic-head cancer.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Evidence and label requirements vary by regimen and setting; confirm the source and pharmacy plan.

    Transplant implications. This is a cancer-treatment roadmap update only. The withdrawn PDAC liver-transplant pathway remains closed; chemotherapy response does not reopen it.

    PAXG — Selected neoadjuvant use

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Cisplatin, nab-paclitaxel, capecitabine and gemcitabine. Consider only with regimen-specific expertise and explicit multidisciplinary agreement; not an automatic replacement for established induction options. Discuss PAXG as an evidence-supported preoperative option for selected patients, with local MDT/formulary adoption still OPEN. Not a blanket replacement for mFOLFIRINOX, not a metastatic comparison, and not a PDAC transplant indication.

    Clinical evidence.
    • Median event-free survival 16.0 versus 10.2 months, HR 0.63 (0.47–0.84). EFS included confirmed CA19-9 rises and unresectability, not just progression/death. Resection 75% versus 67% (not significant); R0 rates similar. Grade ≥3 toxicity 66% versus 61%. OS immature; no established OS superiority.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Open-label, high-volume Italian centers, all White population, age cap. Converted phase II to III after 86% enrollment; no independent monitoring committee. Thirty-three EFS events were marker-only. Do not relabel EFS as OS or PFS.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. This is a cancer-treatment roadmap update only. The withdrawn PDAC liver-transplant pathway remains closed; chemotherapy response does not reopen it.

    Combined HCC CCA — After resection

    cHCC–CCA
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. No established adjuvant systemic standard specific to this histology. Discuss surveillance, trial participation or an individualized borrowed regimen in MDT.

    Clinical evidence.
    • Do not describe BILCAP, PRODIGE 24 or HCC adjuvant evidence as direct cHCC-CCA evidence. Record the uncertainty in the decision document.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Evidence and label requirements vary by regimen and setting; confirm the source and pharmacy plan.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Combined HCC-CCA is not interchangeable with pure HCC or pure BTC. Regimen borrowing and any transplant proposal require explicit multidisciplinary rationale; these data do not validate a new LT cutoff.

    Trials and supporting sources (1)
    • Hong 2026 review · Hong JY · Journal of liver cancer · 2026PMID 41781152 · DOI 10.17998/jlc.2026.03.02 · TMC Library

    Combination / sequencing evidence

    Systemic therapy combined with TACE

    HCC
    Selected multidisciplinary or trial consideration

    When to consider. TACE-eligible unresectable HCC: eligibility differs by regimen. LEAP-012 and EMERALD-3 mainly required Child-Pugh A; EMERALD-1 allowed B7. Evaluate current guideline position and competing curative options.

    Clinical evidence.
    • EMERALD-1, LEAP-012 and EMERALD-3 reported progression-free survival benefit for their respective combinations.
    • In EMERALD-3, STRIDE + lenvatinib + TACE yielded PFS 13.0 versus 9.8 months; overall-survival superiority was not established at the reported analysis.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. PFS benefit is not proof of OS benefit or a transplant bridge. LEAP-012 grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicity was 71% vs 32%; EMERALD-3 grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity was 63% vs 19%. EMERALD-1 durvalumab without bevacizumab did not improve PFS.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. For a listed patient with treatable liver-limited disease, use LRT for routine bridging. Adding systemic treatment has no demonstrated benefit for dropout or transplant receipt. In embolization-eligible unresectable HCC, reported follow-up showed median overall survival of 40.4 vs 40.8 months in LEAP-012 (HR 0.98) and 29.9 vs 33.3 months in EMERALD-1 (HR 1.10). Neither trial measured waitlist dropout or transplant receipt.

Roadmaps / Treatment matrices · systemic therapy by tumor type

Systemic therapy matrix

Choose a tumor and a treatment setting. Each card shows when to consider a regimen and its trial results, with every PMID linked to the full citation; open Limits, Transplant or Sources for the rest.

Multidisciplinary review aid, not prescribing orders. Cross-trial survival medians do not rank treatments.

Clinical review draft · Evidence reviewed through 25 October 2026.

Choose by tumor type, stage, prior treatment, biomarkers, organ function and patient goals. Trial results retain their own populations and comparators; cross-trial survival medians do not rank treatments. This matrix supports multidisciplinary discussion and does not provide prescribing orders.

Settings

Colour marks the treatment setting — its place in the treatment sequence. It is not an evidence grade or a ranking.

Treatment options by setting

Initial advanced-disease treatment

Atezolizumab + bevacizumab

HCC
Preferred first-line option

When to consider. Unresectable HCC requiring systemic treatment; strongest evidence in Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1. Assess and treat high-risk varices before bevacizumab.

Clinical evidence.
  • IMbrave150: updated median overall survival 19.2 versus 13.4 months with sorafenib; HR 0.66.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Bleeding, portal hypertension, blood pressure, proteinuria and immune toxicity affect selection. Do not compare its survival median directly with a different trial.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. If transplant remains possible, review the plan before the first dose. Record both last-dose dates and agree how to handle an early graft offer. Pretransplant series describe selected downstaging and a risk of rejection.

  • IMbrave150 update · Cheng · Journal of Hepatology · 2022PMID 34902530 · DOI 10.1016/j.jhep.2021.11.030 · TMC Library

Durvalumab + tremelimumab (STRIDE)

HCC
Preferred first-line option

When to consider. Unresectable HCC, preserved liver function and fitness for dual checkpoint therapy. An option when bevacizumab is unsuitable and immunotherapy is appropriate.

Clinical evidence.
  • HIMALAYA: median overall survival 16.43 versus 13.77 months with sorafenib; HR 0.78. Progression-free survival was not significantly improved.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Main portal-vein invasion was excluded from the pivotal trial. Immune toxicity remains important; avoiding bevacizumab does not remove treatment risk.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. Requires a transplant-specific plan if transplantation may later be considered.

  • HIMALAYA / STRIDE · Abou-Alfa · NEJM Evidence · 2022PMID 38319892 · DOI 10.1056/EVIDoa2100070 · TMC Library

Nivolumab + ipilimumab

HCC
Preferred first-line option

When to consider. Unresectable HCC; select patients able to tolerate dual checkpoint therapy and close early monitoring.

Clinical evidence.
  • CheckMate 9DW: median overall survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months with lenvatinib or sorafenib; HR 0.79.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Survival curves crossed: mortality was higher during the first six months (HR 1.65). Grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 41% versus 42%; treatment-related deaths were 12 versus 3.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. Review future transplant intent and immune adverse effects before choosing this regimen.

  • CheckMate 9DW · Yau · The Lancet · 2025PMID 40349714 · DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(25)00403-9 · TMC Library

Single-agent checkpoint therapy

HCC
Selected alternative

When to consider. Tislelizumab or durvalumab when a single-agent approach is appropriate. NCCN HCC v2.2026 also lists pembrolizumab first line, category 2B.

Clinical evidence.
  • RATIONALE-301 established overall-survival noninferiority of tislelizumab to sorafenib.
  • HIMALAYA established noninferiority of durvalumab.
  • KEYNOTE-394 supported later-line pembrolizumab in an Asian population;
  • KEYNOTE-240 did not meet its prespecified statistical thresholds.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Guideline options and US indications differ: durvalumab monotherapy is not the labelled HCC regimen; the HCC label specifies combination treatment. KEYNOTE-240/394 are later-line studies, not first-line superiority evidence.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. Single-agent checkpoint therapy still carries transplant rejection concerns.

Lenvatinib or sorafenib

HCC
Alternative when immunotherapy is unsuitable

When to consider. Unresectable HCC with adequate liver reserve; consider when checkpoint therapy is contraindicated or inconsistent with the transplant plan.

Clinical evidence.
  • REFLECT: lenvatinib vs sorafenib OS 13.6 vs 12.3 months; noninferiority design.
  • SHARP: sorafenib vs placebo OS 10.7 vs 7.9 months, HR 0.69 (0.55–0.87); radiologic time to progression 5.5 vs 2.8 months, not PFS.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. REFLECT enrolled Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1 and excluded main portal-vein invasion, ≥50% liver occupation and obvious bile-duct invasion. SHARP reported grade 3 diarrhea and hand–foot reaction of 8% each with sorafenib; these are not lenvatinib toxicity rates. Little evidence supports use in decompensated cirrhosis.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. When local treatment is infeasible or has failed, review systemic treatment with the transplant team. In two small bridging trials, adding sorafenib to TACE or Y90 showed no clear transplant benefit. In the Y90 pilot, all 10 sorafenib patients needed a dose reduction. Biliary complications within 30 days occurred in 4/8 combination recipients vs 0/9 with Y90 alone.

Gemcitabine + cisplatin + durvalumab or pembrolizumab

pCCA / iCCA
Preferred first-line options

When to consider. Unresectable or metastatic biliary cancer after addressing biliary obstruction, infection, renal function and performance status.

Clinical evidence.
  • TOPAZ-1: overall-survival HR 0.80 for durvalumab + chemotherapy versus chemotherapy.
  • KEYNOTE-966: median overall survival 12.7 versus 10.9 months, HR 0.83, with pembrolizumab added.
Limits of the evidence

Limits of the evidence. Mixed biliary-tract populations; neither trial establishes a separate pCCA-specific effect or superiority between these two checkpoint regimens. ASCO 2026.1.0 is an advanced-BTC systemic guideline, not a transplant-neoadjuvant or eligibility guideline.

Transplant implications

Transplant implications. For potentially transplant-eligible pCCA or iCCA, obtain transplant-program review first. Palliative chemoimmunotherapy is not an interchangeable transplant neoadjuvant protocol.

Gemcitabine + cisplatin; adapt intensity when necessary

pCCA / iCCA
When checkpoint therapy is unsuitable

When to consider. Use chemotherapy alone when immunotherapy is unsuitable. Renal impairment, neuropathy, hearing loss or frailty may require a different platinum, regimen or single agent after oncology review.

Clinical evidence.

Transplant implications. An approved transplant regimen may use chemotherapy differently; confirm the protocol before starting treatment.

Transplant implications. Combined HCC-CCA is not interchangeable with pure HCC or pure BTC. Regimen borrowing and any transplant proposal require explicit multidisciplinary rationale; these data do not validate a new LT cutoff.

    177Lu-DOTATATE peptide receptor radionuclide therapy

    NELM / pNET
    Progressive SSTR-positive, well-differentiated disease

    When to consider. Confirm adequate receptor uptake, renal function and marrow reserve. NETTER-1 directly studied progressive midgut NET despite a somatostatin analogue.

    Clinical evidence.
    • NETTER-1: 20-month PFS 65.2% versus 10.8% with high-dose octreotide.
    • Final median OS 48.0 versus 36.3 months was not statistically significant (HR 0.84; p=0.30).

    Limits of the evidence. Long-term risks include marrow toxicity and uncommon myelodysplasia/leukemia. Primary site and prior therapy affect applicability. NETTER-1 enrolled midgut NET; its numerical results are not pancreatic-NET-specific estimates.

    Transplant implications. Record disease control and treatment toxicity before any transplant benefit review. PRRT response does not expand accepted grade or spread criteria.

    Everolimus or sunitinib

    NELM / pNET
    Progressive disease; primary site determines the option

    When to consider. Everolimus: pancreatic NET or appropriate nonfunctional GI/lung NET. Sunitinib: pancreatic NET.

    Clinical evidence.
    • RADIANT-3: PFS 11.0 versus 4.6 months in pancreatic NET.
    • RADIANT-4: PFS 11.0 versus 3.9 months in nonfunctional GI/lung NET.
    • Sunitinib trial: PFS 11.4 versus 5.5 months in pancreatic NET.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Trials used placebo comparators, not contemporary PRRT/CAPTEM sequencing. Monitor infection/pneumonitis/metabolic toxicity with everolimus and vascular/cardiac toxicity with sunitinib.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. The efficacy of nontransplant options must be considered before exposing a recipient and donor to transplantation.

    Cabozantinib

    NELM / pNET
    Previously treated, progressive well-differentiated NET

    When to consider. Pancreatic or extrapancreatic NET after appropriate prior treatment.

    Clinical evidence.
    • CABINET: median PFS 13.8 versus 4.4 months in pancreatic NET and 8.4 versus 3.9 months in extrapancreatic NET, each compared with placebo.

    Limits of the evidence. The two cohorts are distinct; do not pool their effect sizes. Toxicity and dose reductions are common. PFS benefit does not establish an OS advantage.

    Transplant implications. An additional effective nontransplant option changes the benefit discussion, not the transplant criteria.

    Liposomal irinotecan fluorouracil leucovorin or switch backbone — Subsequent treatment

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. nal-IRI plus 5-FU/LV after gemcitabine-based therapy when eligible. Gemcitabine-based therapy may follow a fluoropyrimidine regimen. Account for prior irinotecan and residual neuropathy. Use the combination after gemcitabine when fit; avoid treating nal-IRI as interchangeable with conventional irinotecan. Dose conventions differ: 70 mg/m² free base equals 80 mg/m² salt in the publication. Pharmacy must verify the actual product/order set.

    Clinical evidence.
    • nal-IRI plus 5-FU/LV: OS 6.1 versus 4.2 months, HR 0.67 (0.49–0.92); PFS 3.1 versus 1.5, HR 0.56. ORR 16% versus 1%. nal-IRI monotherapy did not improve OS (HR 0.99). Grade 3–4 neutropenia 27%, diarrhea 13%.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Small prior-irinotecan subgroup, different 5-FU schedules, selected organ function. No validated immediate reuse after FOLFIRINOX/NALIRIFOX. One combination treatment-related septic-shock death.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. This is a cancer-treatment roadmap update only. The withdrawn PDAC liver-transplant pathway remains closed; chemotherapy response does not reopen it.

    Liposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil leucovorin — Selected later line

    iCCA / pCCA
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Discuss only with an explicit explanation of the inconsistent randomized evidence, prior irinotecan exposure, bilirubin and diarrhea risk. Not an interchangeable default with FOLFOX. Show NALIRICC alongside NIFTY. Do not call nal-IRI/5-FU an unqualified preferred second-line BTC regimen. Consider only a qualified alternative after target review, especially if oxaliplatin is unsuitable, with explicit benefit/toxicity discussion.

    Clinical evidence.
    • PFS 2.6 versus 2.3 months, HR 0.87 (0.56–1.35); OS 6.9 versus 8.2 months, HR 1.08 (0.68–1.72). ORR 14% versus 4% did not translate into PFS/OS benefit. Grade ≥3 events 71% versus 50%; treatment-related serious events 33% versus 2%.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Small phase II trial; subsequent therapy differed (more control patients received later therapy). This does not erase the negative primary PFS result. Contrasts with positive NIFTY; population and treatment differences do not resolve the inconsistency.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. Systemic disease control is not proof of transplant benefit. Preserve the route-specific histology, liver-only status, unresectability and observation gates. A cHCC-CCA component changes the evidence base; use expert pathology review.

    pCCA / iCCA
    Usual adjuvant discussion

    When to consider. Resected biliary cancer after recovery; discuss approximately six months of adjuvant treatment and margin-specific radiation considerations.

    Perioperative chemotherapy around liver resection

    CRLM
    Individualize with the liver multidisciplinary team

    When to consider. Resectable CRLM: balance recurrence risk, prior treatment, liver injury and surgical timing. Surgery-first or perioperative chemotherapy may be appropriate.

    • EORTC 40983 showed PFS signals in eligible/resected analyses; its intention-to-treat PFS comparison and long-term OS comparison were not significant.

    Limits of the evidence. Do not use metastatic anti-EGFR response data to justify routine perioperative cetuximab for resectable CRLM. Exploratory molecular subtypes from New EPOC are not validated selectors for transplantation.

    Transplant implications. Resectability is reviewed before a transplant route. Radiographic disappearance alone does not prove eradication.

    PAXG — Selected neoadjuvant use

    PDAC
    Setting-specific MDT option

    When to consider. Cisplatin, nab-paclitaxel, capecitabine and gemcitabine. Consider only with regimen-specific expertise and explicit multidisciplinary agreement; not an automatic replacement for established induction options. Discuss PAXG as an evidence-supported preoperative option for selected patients, with local MDT/formulary adoption still OPEN. Not a blanket replacement for mFOLFIRINOX, not a metastatic comparison, and not a PDAC transplant indication.

    Clinical evidence.
    • Median event-free survival 16.0 versus 10.2 months, HR 0.63 (0.47–0.84). EFS included confirmed CA19-9 rises and unresectability, not just progression/death. Resection 75% versus 67% (not significant); R0 rates similar. Grade ≥3 toxicity 66% versus 61%. OS immature; no established OS superiority.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Open-label, high-volume Italian centers, all White population, age cap. Converted phase II to III after 86% enrollment; no independent monitoring committee. Thirty-three EFS events were marker-only. Do not relabel EFS as OS or PFS.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. This is a cancer-treatment roadmap update only. The withdrawn PDAC liver-transplant pathway remains closed; chemotherapy response does not reopen it.

    Combination / sequencing evidence

    Systemic therapy combined with TACE

    HCC
    Selected multidisciplinary or trial consideration

    When to consider. TACE-eligible unresectable HCC: eligibility differs by regimen. LEAP-012 and EMERALD-3 mainly required Child-Pugh A; EMERALD-1 allowed B7. Evaluate current guideline position and competing curative options.

    Clinical evidence.
    • EMERALD-1: durvalumab + bevacizumab + TACE vs TACE improved PFS (15.0 vs 8.2 months, HR 0.77).
    • Final OS was 29.9 vs 33.3 months (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.87–1.39, ESMO GI 2026, 183O).
    • LEAP-012: lenvatinib + pembrolizumab + TACE vs TACE improved PFS (14.6 vs 10.0 months, HR 0.66).
    • Long-term OS was 40.4 vs 40.8 months (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.76–1.26, ESMO 2026, 1678RO).
    • EMERALD-3: STRIDE + lenvatinib + TACE vs TACE improved PFS (13.0 vs 9.8 months). Interim OS HR 0.84 did not meet the prespecified significance boundary.
    Limits of the evidence

    Limits of the evidence. Grade ≥3 treatment-related events were 71% vs 32% in the primary LEAP-012 analysis. Grade 3–4 treatment-related events were 63% vs 19% in EMERALD-3. Durvalumab without bevacizumab did not improve PFS in EMERALD-1.

    Transplant implications

    Transplant implications. For a listed patient with treatable liver-limited HCC, use liver-directed therapy for routine bridging. These phase 3 trials did not test waitlist dropout or transplant receipt.
